title: How commercial loan brokers find more lenders, and the right one for each file
summary: Where commercial loan brokers find lenders that work with brokers, how to read a lender’s credit box, and why a lender-criteria matrix beats shotgunning files.
body_markdown:
A site-work contractor in Texas wants $185,000 for a used excavator. It has been in business three years, the owner’s credit is decent, and the dealer would like an answer soon. You have a list of lenders. The contractor and every number here are invented, but the moment is familiar.


The tempting move is to send the file to everyone on the list and see who bites. The better move is to know, before you send anything, which of those lenders would even look at a three-year-old construction business buying a ten-year-old machine. Most of this guide is about getting to that point: where brokers find lenders, how to pin down what each one actually funds, and how to keep that knowledge in a form you can use on the next file.


Quick answer


Commercial loan brokers build a lender panel from five places: direct lenders’ broker programs, equipment finance funders, SBA lenders, CDFIs and state lending programs. Many of the introductions happen through associations such as NEFA and AACFB, whose members include both brokers and funding sources.\[1,2\]


Finding names is the easy half. The work that pays is learning each lender’s credit box, keeping it in a matrix, and sending every file only to the lenders it fits.


Key takeaways


-


A lender panel is worth the credit boxes it covers, not the number of names on it.


-


Public data helps you find lenders who already make loans like yours: SBA publishes approved 7(a) and 504 loans with the lender, state, industry and amount, and the CDFI Fund publishes its list of certified CDFIs.


-


Write each lender’s credit box down, date it, and correct it from every decline.


-


Send each file only to the lenders it fits, complete and honestly disclosed. That is what keeps a lender reading your next one.


01


## Why fit matters more than the size of your list


“How many lenders do you work with?” is a question brokers get asked and ask each other. It is the wrong measure. A list of sixty lenders that all want two-year-old businesses borrowing $250,000 to $2 million does nothing for a start-up asking for $90,000. Twelve lenders whose boxes cover different sizes, industries and credit profiles are likely to cover more of the files you actually see.


Shotgunning a file has costs that do not show up on the day you send it. Each submission takes an underwriter’s time, and many lenders pull the owner’s credit when they review a file. A lender that keeps receiving files outside its box learns that your files are not screened, and reads the next one with that in mind. And a borrower who hears from six lenders in a week starts to wonder who is running the process.


So the useful version of “find more lenders” is narrower: find the lenders who cover the files you are not placing today. Look back at the last twenty deals you lost or never sent. If most of them were under two years in business, or in one industry, or in one state, that is the gap your next lender relationship should fill.


02


## Where brokers find lenders that work with brokers


There is no single directory of lenders that take broker deals. Most brokers build their panel from the same five sources, and use each for a different kind of file.


### Direct lenders’ broker and ISO programs


Many banks and non-bank lenders run a program for outside originators, often called a broker, partner or ISO program. Joining one usually means an application, a signed agreement and some vetting of you and your business. What you get in return matters more than the agreement: a program guide that spells out the credit box, a named contact who can answer questions before you submit, and a submission checklist. If a lender cannot give you those, you will learn its box one decline at a time.


### Equipment finance funders and their associations


Equipment finance has the most developed broker channel, and its trade associations are where brokers and funders meet. The National Equipment Finance Association counts independent and bank-owned lessors and funding sources, commercial finance brokers and specialty lenders among its members, and runs conferences through the year.\[1\] The American Association of Commercial Finance Brokers describes itself as a trade association for independent commercial finance professionals and their funding source partners.\[2\] Its Meet the Funder webinars have funding sources explain who makes their decisions and what their policies are, which is exactly the information a broker needs.\[3\]


The Equipment Leasing and Finance Association is the industry’s larger trade body, with members drawn from financial services companies, manufacturers and service providers.\[4\] Its membership is a useful map of who funds equipment, and its events are another place to meet them.


### SBA lenders, found through SBA’s own data


For SBA’s main program the lender is a private institution: SBA says 7(a) loans are delivered by SBA 7(a) lenders.\[5\] The useful part for a broker is that SBA publishes loan-level data on approved 7(a) and 504 loans, refreshed quarterly. Each record carries the lender’s name, the project’s state, the borrower’s industry code, the approved amount and the age of the business.\[6\]


Filter it to your state, your borrowers’ industries and your deal sizes, and you have a list of lenders who have actually made loans like yours, rather than lenders who say they do. SBA also publishes a lender report that summarizes approvals by state and lender, if you want the short version.\[7\]


Before you call, read the program’s rules. Kita’s[lending programs hub](https://www.kita.ai/lending-programs) sets out the borrower eligibility, lender requirements and underwriting requirements for[SBA 7(a)](https://www.kita.ai/lending-programs/sba-7a) ,[SBA Express](https://www.kita.ai/lending-programs/sba-express) and[SBA 504](https://www.kita.ai/lending-programs/sba-504) , each with its official source. SBA’s rules define a referral agent as someone who refers an applicant to a lender or a lender to an applicant, which is the role most brokers play, and set standards for agents who deal with SBA on a borrower’s behalf.\[11\]


### CDFIs


Community development financial institutions are certified by the Treasury’s CDFI Fund and provide financial services in low-income communities and to people who lack access to financing. They include community development banks, credit unions and loan funds.\[9\] The CDFI Fund publishes its list of certified CDFIs, which can be sorted by name, location and type and includes contact details for each.\[10\]


CDFIs can be a home for files that sit just outside a bank’s box: younger businesses, thinner credit, owners in underserved markets. Check geography first. The CDFI Fund notes that some serve only their own city or town, while others cover neighboring counties or whole states.\[10\]


### State and other government programs


State capital access, loan guarantee, participation and collateral support programs, many of them funded through[SSBCI](https://www.kita.ai/lending-programs/ssbci) , work through private lenders that enroll in them. A lender that uses one of those programs may be able to say yes to a file it would otherwise decline. The[lending programs hub](https://www.kita.ai/lending-programs) lists the programs by state, for example[California](https://www.kita.ai/lending-programs/states/california) , with the rules for each.


### A note on SBA Lender Match


Your borrowers can find SBA lenders without you. SBA’s Lender Match tool has more than 800 participating lenders and returns a list of interested lenders within two business days. SBA is clear that it is not a loan application and does not guarantee a match or a loan.\[8\] That is worth remembering: the value a broker adds is not a list of names. It is knowing which lender fits, presenting the file well and seeing it through.


03


## How to read a lender’s credit box


A credit box is the set of deals a lender will consider. Program guides describe it, but they leave out the details that decide most files, and they go out of date. The way to pin a box down is to ask the same questions of every lender, in the same order, and write the answers down.


The nine parts of a lender’s credit box and what to ask about each Part of the box What to ask the lender Why it matters


Deal size What is your smallest and largest deal, and where do you stop doing application-only? A floor or a ceiling is the first filter on any file, and the easiest decline to avoid.


Products Which do you actually fund: equipment, term loans, working capital, lines, SBA? A lender that lists six products may only be competitive in two of them.


Industries Which industries are restricted or excluded, and which do you like? The same industry can be excluded by one lender and sought by another.


Time in business What is your minimum, and do you treat a change of ownership as a new business? Start-ups and recent acquisitions are where boxes differ most.


Owner credit and history How do you treat a past bankruptcy, a tax lien or a recent late payment? Better to learn it before the file goes in than from the decline.


Cash flow How do you measure repayment: tax returns, bank statements, interim statements? It decides what you collect and whether this borrower’s numbers will read well.


Collateral and equity Do you need titled equipment, a down payment, real estate or a personal guarantee? Used, soft-cost or private-party equipment is a common dividing line.


Geography Which states do you lend in, and are any excluded? Banks and CDFIs often lend in a defined area; some funders exclude states.


Documentation What does a complete submission look like for a deal this size? The answer is your checklist. An incomplete file usually comes back with questions before anyone reads it.


Two more questions are worth asking every lender. What have you declined lately, and why? And what does a file look like that you were glad to see? The first tells you where the box has moved since the program guide was printed. The second tells you what a strong submission looks like to that particular credit team.


04


## Keep a lender-criteria matrix


The answers belong in one place: a matrix with a row for each lender and a column for each part of the box. A spreadsheet is enough. What matters is that it is complete, dated, and checked before every submission, not reconstructed from memory.

Read against the contractor’s file, five lenders become two. Funder C’s floor is above the request, Funder D does not lend in Texas and Funder E excludes construction. Funder B fits on every column. Funder A fits on everything except the age of the machine, which sits right at its limit, so the right move is a call before the file goes in. Two submissions instead of five, and neither of them wasted.


A few habits keep the matrix useful:


-


**Date every row.** A credit box you confirmed eight months ago is a guess. Re-confirm the oldest rows first.


-


**Write the decline reason in.** Every decline tells you something about the box. If a lender declines two restaurants in a row, add it to the industry column, even if the guide does not say so.


-


**Record the documents each lender wants at each size.** It becomes your collection checklist for the borrower, so you ask once instead of three times.


-


**Keep a column for what you have observed.** How quickly a lender answered your questions and how clearly it explained a decline are worth noting, as your own records rather than anyone’s promise.


-


**Look at the empty spaces.** Files that fit no row are the clearest guide to which lender to add next.


05


## Keeping lender relationships healthy


A lender relationship is built file by file. Three habits do most of the work.


### Send clean, complete submissions


Send everything on the lender’s checklist the first time, labeled so an underwriter can find each document without opening every one. Add a short cover note: what the business does, what the money is for, how it will be repaid, and what is weak in the file and why you still think it fits. An underwriter who has to come back with a list of questions before reading the file will remember that the next time your name appears.


### Disclose what you know


If you know about a past default, a tax lien, recent financing from another lender or a figure that does not tie out, say so in the cover note. Lenders usually find these things, and finding one you did not mention costs you more than the file. The law is plain about the extreme case: a knowingly false statement made to influence SBA, an FDIC-insured bank or a credit union on a loan application is a federal crime.\[12\] On SBA loans, SBA can also suspend or revoke an agent’s privilege to deal with it, for conduct that includes steering an applicant to another firm’s services without disclosing a business relationship with it.\[11\]


### Close the loop


Tell a lender when a deal is withdrawn or has closed elsewhere, so its team stops working on it. Ask for the reason behind every decline and write it into the matrix. Be straight when a lender asks where else a file has gone. And when a lender takes a fair look at a hard file, send it the next one that fits its box.

## Frequently asked questions


### How do commercial loan brokers find lenders?


Most brokers build a panel from five places: the broker or ISO programs that direct lenders run, the broker channels of equipment finance companies, SBA lenders, CDFIs and state lending programs. Industry associations such as NEFA and AACFB, whose members include both brokers and funding sources, are where many of those introductions happen. SBA’s public loan data shows which lenders actually make SBA loans in a given state, industry and size, and the CDFI Fund publishes a list of certified CDFIs.


### Do lenders work with commercial loan brokers?


Many do, and many do not. Plenty of banks, equipment finance companies and non-bank lenders take broker-referred deals through a dedicated program with its own application and rules, while others only originate directly. SBA’s own rules define a referral agent as someone who refers an applicant to a lender or a lender to an applicant. Ask each lender whether it takes broker submissions, and what it needs from you before you send a file.


### How many lenders should a commercial loan broker have?


There is no right number. What matters is that the lenders on your panel, taken together, cover the files you actually see: your deal sizes, your borrowers’ industries and time in business, and the collateral they bring. A short list of lenders whose credit boxes you know well usually serves borrowers better than a long list you have never tested.


### What is a lender’s credit box?


A credit box is the set of deals a lender will consider: its minimum and maximum deal size, the products it funds, the industries it excludes, its minimum time in business, how it treats owner credit history, how it measures cash flow, the collateral it needs, the states it lends in and the documents it requires. Brokers learn it from the lender’s program guide, from conversations with the lender and from the reasons given for declines.


### Should a broker send the same file to several lenders at once?


Sending a file to every lender on the list wastes underwriters’ time, can mean more credit inquiries on the owner and teaches lenders that your files are not screened. Send each file to the lenders whose credit box it fits, in a complete package, and be straight with a lender who asks where else the file has gone.


### What should a broker disclose to a lender?


Everything that is material to the credit: past defaults or bankruptcies, tax liens, other recent financing, and any problem you noticed in the documents. Lenders usually find these on their own, and a knowingly false statement made to influence SBA, an FDIC-insured bank or a credit union is a federal crime. For SBA loans, SBA can also suspend or revoke an agent’s privilege to deal with it, for example over an undisclosed business relationship.
